REPORT OF OPERATIONS
Port Lease Transaction
On 31 October 2016 a 50-year lease of land and assets comprised in the Port of Melbourne commenced between
Melbourne Port Lessor Pty Ltd ('the Company') and a private company owned by the Lonsdale Consortium.
The Company, having granted a lease and becoming entitled to the lease proceeds, recognised a lease receivable
on the same date. The lease receivable was transferred to the State of Victoria's Victorian Transport Fund
('VTF') and treated as a redemption of contributed capital. The lease proceeds received from the Lonsdale
Consortium were deposited directly into the VTF. The VTF is a trust fund within the public account
administered by the Department of Treasury and Finance ('DTF') on behalf of the Treasurer of Victoria.

provides public services, using a service concession asset, on behalf of the grantor and importantly, the operator
manages at least some of the public service at its own discretion. The grantor must also control the asset for AASB
1059 to apply. The grantor controls the asset if, and only if:
(a) the grantor controls or regulates what services the operator must provide with the asset, to whom it must
provide them, and at what price; and
(b) the grantor controls any significant residual interest in the asset at the end of the term of the arrangement.
The Company acknowledges that the application of AASB 1059 is complex and highly judgemental. The Company has
undertaken a comprehensive assessment of its Port of Melbourne lease arrangement entered with the Lonsdale
Consortium, including obtaining independent advice, to assess whether the port lease arrangement falls within the scope
of AASB 1059.

Areas of significant judgement involve:
• the unit of account for the Company's port assets;
the nature of the services provided by the assets (i.e. whether it is a public service); and
• the extent of regulation of those assets and how significant this regulation is in the transaction.
The Company considers:
The port assets are assessed to belong to one cash-generating unit (CGU). This CGU includes both assets
providing Prescribed Services and assets providing Non-Prescribed Services.
Prescribed Services include:
the provision of channels (except anchorages) for use by shipping in port of Melbourne waters;
the provision of berths, buoys, or dolphins in connection with the berthing of vessels;
the provision of short-term storage or cargo marshalling facilities in connection with the loading or
unloading of vessels at berths, buoys or dolphins in the port of Melbourne;
- the provision of access to, or allowing the uses of, places or infrastructure on port of Melbourne land for
the provision of services to port users; and
any other service that is prescribed by the regulations.
Non-Prescribed Services relate to leasing activities.
The current regulatory framework and lease agreement does not provide the State of Victoria with sufficient
iї.
control of the non-prescribed services (i.e. leasing activities) provided by the port assets as envisaged under
AASB 1059. Considering all relevant matters, the leasing activities are both quantitatively and qualitatively
significant in the context of the AASB 1059 assessment. Therefore, it is the Company's view that the
regulation at the port is not substantive enough when considering the control of asset during the lease term.
The leasing activities at the port are substantive enough for the whole arrangement to fall outside of the scope
of AASB 1059. The inability to control a significant and inseparable part of the asset is considered to result in
the whole arrangement falling outside the scope of AASB 1059.
Based on the above the Company has concluded that the port lease arrangement falls outside of the scope of AASB
1059, and the arrangement will continue to be accounted for as a lease under AASB 16 Leases (AASB 16).
The Company notes that with the practical application of AASB 1059 continuing to evolve and as more experience is
gained in applying the standard, the application to the Company may be revisited. Should AASB 1059 apply in future
reporting periods, in whole or in part to the port assets, the valuation methodology for valuing the assets subject to the
service concession arrangement will need to be revisited to determine whether there would be any difference between
the current carrying value and the current replacement cost.

the Company performs a managerial assessment to estimate possible changes in fair value of since the date of the last
independent valuation with reference to available data. Fair value assessments for land and buildings are determined

An impairment loss of a revalued asset is treated as a revaluation decrease. The decrease shall be recognised in the

Land comprises freehold allotments which together form nine non-contiguous precincts, extending from Port Phillip

revaluation of land was performed utilising the market and income approach. The market approach references market
evidence including observable sales data for properties in similar localities and adjusted for size, location, zoning and
features of other sites compared with the features of the land. The income approach discounts future net rental
cashflows plus terminal value to present value at a market discount rate.
For the financial year ended 30 June 2026, the roll-forward revaluation exercise was performed utilising the income
approach. The cash flow forecasts provided for land from the 30 June 2025 revaluation exercise was used to undertake
the 30 June 2026 fair value assessment, adjusted for known contractual items such as inflationary adjustments.
Since the fair value determined through the roll-forward revaluation exercise had neither moved by 40% or more from
the previous scheduled revaluation at 30 June 2025 nor differed by more than 10% from the assets' carrying value at
30 June 2026, no revaluation adjustment was recognised. The fair value of the land at 30 June 2026 was determined to
be $5,300 million (2025: $5,300 million).

reference to similar port assets. Whereas an estimated reproduction cost approach (i.e. an indirect cost approach) has

7. RISK, CONTINGENCIES AND VALUATION JUDGEMENTS
7.1 Financial instrument specific disclosures
Introduction
Financial instruments arise out of contractual agreements that give rise to a financial asset of one entity and a financial
liability or equity instrument of another entity.
Categories of financial instruments
Financial assets at amortised cost:
Financial assets measured at amortised cost are financial instruments which meet both of the following criteria and are
not designated at fair value through comprehensive income:
• the financial asset is held within a business model whose objective is to hold financial assets in order to
collect contractual cash flows; and
• the assets' contractual terms give rise on specified dates to cash flows that are solely payments of principal
and interest on the principal amount outstanding.
These assets are initially recognised at fair value plus any directly attributable transaction costs and subsequently
measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method less any impairment.
The Company recognises the following financial assets in this category:
• cash and cash equivalents
• receivables (excluding statutory receivables); and
• term deposits (classified under 'investments and other financial assets')
Financial liabilities at amortised cost:
Financial liabilities at amortised cost are initially recognised on the date they are originated. They are initially
measured at fair value plus any directly attributable transaction costs. Subsequent to initial recognition, these financial
instruments are measured at amortised cost with any difference between the initial recognised amount and the
redemption value being recognised in profit and loss over the period of the interest-bearing liability, using the
effective interest rate method. Financial liabilities at amortised cost include the Company's borrowings and payables
(excluding statutory payables).
Offsetting financial instruments:
Financial instrument assets and liabilities are offset, and the net amount presented in the balance sheet when, and only
when, the Company has a legal right to offset the amounts and intend either to settle on a net basis or to realise the
asset and settle the liability simultaneously. Where the Company does not have a legally enforceable right to offset
recognised amounts, because the right to offset is enforceable only on the occurrence of future events such as default,
insolvency, or bankruptcy, they are reported on a gross basis.
Derecognition of financial assets:'
A financial asset (or, where applicable, a part of a financial asset or part of a group of similar financial assets) is
derecognised when:
• the rights to receive cash flows from the asset have expired; or
• the Company retains the right to receive cash flows from the asset, but has assumed an obligation to pay them
in full without material delay to a third party under a 'pass through' arrangement; or
• the Company has transferred its rights to receive cash flows from the asset and either:
• has transferred substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset; or
o has neither transterred nor retained substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset but has
transferred control of the asset.
Where the Company has neither transferred nor retained substantially all the risks and rewards or transferred control,
the asset is recognised to the extent of the Company's continuing involvement in the asset.

AASB 9 establishes three separate approaches for measuring and recognising ECL:
• A general approach that applies to all loans and receivables not eligible for the other approaches;
• A simplified approach that is required for certain trade receivables and lease receivables; and
• A 'credit adjusted approach that applies to loans that are credit impaired at initial recognition (e.g. loans
acquired at a deep discount due to their credit risk). A distinguishing factor among the approaches is whether
the allowance for expected credit losses at any balance sheet date is calculated by considering possible
defaults only for the next 12 months ('12 month ECLS'), or for the entirc remaining life of the asset
('Lifetime ECLS').

recognised. Under the general approach, the loss allowance is based on 12-month ECLs unless a significant increase in
credit risk occurs. In this case, loss allowance is measured based on lifetime ECLs unless the increase reverses.

AASB 2024-2 amends AASB 7 Finuncial Instruments: Disclosures and AASB 9 Financial Instruments.

AASB 18 Presentation and Disclosure of Financial Statements
AASB 18 replaces AASB 101 Presentation of Financial Statements to improve how entities communicate in their
tinancial statements, with a particular focus on information about financial performance in the comprehensive
operating statement.
The key presentation and disclosure requirements established by AASB 18 is the presentation of newly defined
subtotals in the comprehensive operating statement.
AASB 18 applies to annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027 for for-profit entities and applies
to annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2028 for not-for-profit entities. The one-year deferral
allows the AASB to consult with stakeholders and consider potential modifications for not-for-profit public sector
entities. On 30 October 2025, the AASB released Exposure Draft ED 338 Application of AASB 18 and AASB 17 by
Superannuation and Not-for-Profit Entities and Operating Cash Flow Reconciliation, proposing its public sector
modifications to AASB 18 for public comments by 27 February 2026.
The Company is currently in the process of assessing the potential impact of these standards and amendments.
A number of other standards and amendments have also been issued that apply to future reporting periods, however
they are not expected to have any significant impact on the financial statements in the period of initial application.
